nameStory: Greater burdock gets its "greater" name because it's the largest of the burdock species, towering over its smaller cousin, lesser burdock. The name "burdock" comes from "burr" (those prickly seed heads) and "dock" (a large-leaved plant), while "beggar's buttons" refers to how the burrs stick to clothing like unwanted hitchhikers.
description: Greater burdock is a tall, robust biennial plant that can reach 6 feet or more in height. It's easily recognized by its enormous heart-shaped leaves (some as big as dinner plates) and its distinctive purple thistle-like flowers that later become those infamous burrs that stick to everything. This Eurasian immigrant is now found throughout New England, thriving in disturbed soils and waste places where it forms impressive leafy clumps.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Massive heart-shaped leaves that can be over a foot long, with fuzzy undersides that feel like soft flannel and smooth upper surfaces. The leaves grow directly from the base in the first year, creating a impressive rosette.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Purple thistle-like flower heads about the size of a marble, clustered at the tips of branching stems. The flowers have a pleasant, mild fragrance and bloom from July through September.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Brown burrs covered in hooked spines that grab onto clothing, fur, and skin with remarkable tenacity. Each burr contains multiple seeds and makes a distinctive rattling sound when shaken.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a low rosette of giant leaves in year one, then sends up a tall branching flower stalk in year two that can tower over your head. The whole plant has a robust, almost prehistoric appearance.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thick, grooved flower stems that feel sturdy and substantial, often with a reddish tinge. The stems are hollow and make a satisfying snap when broken.

habitat: Greater burdock loves rich, disturbed soils with high nitrogen content, making it common around farmyards, compost piles, and waste areas. You'll find it along roadsides, in abandoned lots, near barns and old homesteads, and anywhere the soil has been enriched by human or animal activity. It particularly thrives in partly shaded areas with moist, fertile soil.

seasonality.spring: First-year plants emerge as rosettes of increasingly large heart-shaped leaves, while second-year plants send up their impressive flowering stalks.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with purple flowers attracting bees and butterflies. The enormous leaves are at their most impressive size during hot summer months.
seasonality.fall: Flowers mature into the notorious burrs that turn brown and become master hitchhikers, while leaves begin to yellow and die back.
seasonality.winter: Dead flower stalks persist with dried burrs still attached, rattling in winter winds and continuing to disperse seeds until spring.

funFact: The hooked burrs of burdock directly inspired the invention of Velcro in 1941, when Swiss engineer George de Mestral examined the burrs stuck to his dog's fur under a microscope and discovered their ingenious hook-and-loop design.
confusionNotes: The enormous leaves might be confused with rhubarb, but burdock leaves are heart-shaped (not just large and oval) and feel fuzzy underneath, while rhubarb leaves are smoother and more crinkled. Remember: "Burdock hearts are fuzzy underneath, rhubarb is smooth and crinkled."
contextualKnowledge: Despite being considered a weed in North America, greater burdock is actually cultivated as a vegetable in Asia, where the roots (called "gobo") are eaten and prized for their crisp texture and earthy flavor. The roots are also used in traditional herbal medicine and can grow over two feet long.
compareHints: Greater burdock is significantly larger than lesser burdock in all aspects - bigger leaves, taller stems, and larger burrs. Lesser burdock typically stays under 4 feet tall with leaves under 8 inches, while greater burdock commonly exceeds 6 feet with foot-long leaves. Woolly burdock is much rarer and has distinctly white-woolly leaf undersides.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Lesser burdock is smaller overall than greater burdock and has shorter leaf stalks, making the heart-shaped leaves appear to sit closer to the stem.
Woolly burdock stands out from greater burdock and lesser burdock primarily by its dense white woolly covering that gives leaves and stems a soft, flannel-like texture.
